content.text: SILIAC, the first computer owned and operated by the University of Sydney, built in the 1950s, was constructed using thermionic devices. Its successor, the KDF9, was built in the late 1960s using solid state devices (transistors). Today's supercomputers are built using integrated circuits.
Assess the impact on computers of each succeeding device, with reference to the differences between each device.
For each of valves, transistors and integrated circuits, write three things: what it is made of, what advantage it brought, and what limitation it introduced.

The top band of the marking scheme wants a judgement about computing power that is supported by the concentration of components on a chip, so make the judgement explicitly rather than leaving it implied.
Finish by linking each generation to the one before it; that link is separately marked and is easy to omit.

Therionic devices, or valves, are large glass envelopes containing a heated cathode that emits electrons, a control grid and an anode. They are large and bulky, they take a long time to warm up and cannot be switched instantly, they consume a great deal of power and produce a great deal of heat, they generate stray magnetic fields, they are fragile and they cannot be made very small. This meant that a computer such as SILIAC occupied a large room, consumed a large amount of power, needed constant supervision and could perform only simple calculations. The transistor, a solid state device made of semiconductor materials such as silicon, has no heated cathode and no vacuum, is tiny, switches almost instantly, consumes very little power, generates almost no heat and has a long life. The consequence was that tens of thousands of transistors could be packed into a small volume, so machines such as the KDF9 were far smaller, faster, cheaper to run and more reliable than valve machines, and the valve was abandoned. The integrated circuit, or chip, goes further by fabricating many transistors together with their interconnections on a single small wafer of silicon, so the number of components per unit area is higher still. Supercomputers now use millions of chips, each containing billions of transistors, and can carry out billions of operations per second in a rack occupying far less space than a single valve of SILIAC, with no warm-up time and negligible power cost per operation. The overall impact has therefore been a progressive increase in speed, memory, reliability and miniaturisation and a progressive decrease in cost, size, power consumption and heat generation, which has made computers accessible for purposes from scientific research to household appliances, and has produced the supercomputers, mobile phones and the internet. The limit of each generation has been the number of components that can be fitted into a given volume, and each advance in the method of fabrication and packing has raised that limit.

Examiners reported that most candidates provided good specific detail, and that good responses contained details as to the specific advantages and disadvantages of each generation of devices and good closing summaries that made judgements about their impact on computers.

content.text: Inverting and summing amplifiers
Explain the use of the three resistors in the summing amplifier shown in Diagram 3.

The two input resistors set the gain and isolate the two signal sources from each other: they convert the input voltages $V_1 = 0.2\,\mathrm{V}$ and $V_2 = 0.1\,\mathrm{V}$ into currents $I_1 = V_1/R_1$ and $I_2 = V_2/R_2$ that flow into the virtual earth point at the inverting input, so the total current entering that node is $I_1 + I_2$ and the output is a weighted sum because the two resistances differ. The $300\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor is the negative feedback resistor: it connects the output back to the inverting input and, because the op-amp has a very high gain, the amplifier adjusts its output until the feedback current exactly equals the summed input current, holding the inverting input at the same potential as the non-inverting input, which is at 0 V. That virtual earth makes the gain predictable and independent of the op-amp, raises the input impedance seen by the signals, reduces output impedance, noise and distortion, widens the bandwidth and stabilises the gain.
